posts.description:
A test fails. You rerun it and it passes. Was there a defect? Was the test updated incorrectly? Or did the result change for no apparent reason?

That last case is flakiness: an automated test producing inconsistent results across executions on the same build, environment and inputs.

The issue is not one occasional false failure. When pass rates oscillate, every failure must be triaged twice: first to establish whether it is real, then to fix it if it is. The suite becomes harder to trust and harder to read.

Read the blog to understand why flaky tests are a strategic problem, not just a tactical annoyance: https://lnkd.in/es8uGkjC

#TestAutomation #SoftwareTesting #QualityAssurance

posts.description:
🧩 A flaky test is frustrating. A test suite full of them becomes a management problem.

Small teams can often investigate failures one at a time, using CI logs, spreadsheets, dashboards, and institutional knowledge to decide which results deserve attention. As the suite grows, that approach makes it harder to see broader patterns and distinguish an unstable test from a genuine product regression.

The result is declining confidence in test results, more frustration for engineers, and greater release risk for the business.

In his latest blog post, Leapwork CTO Rohit Raghuvansi explains why managing flakiness at scale requires more than fixing individual tests. He explores:
💡 Why organization-wide flakiness demands a more strategic approach
💡 How limited context makes recurring patterns difficult to identify
💡 Why ownership and governance are essential to sustainable test management

Read Rohit’s full post: https://lnkd.in/d7WW8XyB.

Every engineer has argued with a flaky test at some point. Re-run it, it passes, nobody investigates further, everyone moves on. That habit is a bigger problem than most of us treat it as.

Flaky tests rarely stay contained to where they started either. A single unstable test in a shared dependency can show up as random failures in projects that have nothing to do with where the actual problem lives. Same test, different behavior depending on where and when it runs. That's what makes it so easy to write off as "just flaky" instead of actually debugging it, because the failure doesn't reproduce the same way twice.

Nobody treats a flaky test like a real bug. It gets re-run, it gets tagged "known flaky," eventually it gets skipped in CI entirely. Nobody traces it back to what's actually causing the instability, because it technically passes if you just try again.

Most of the time it's not exotic. Async waits are usually the biggest cause, a test reads a result before it's actually ready. Concurrency issues come next, almost always two threads fighting over the same in-memory object, not a file or a database like you'd expect. It's mostly a timing assumption that was wrong from the start, just wrong in a way that only shows up sometimes.

What's actually worked for teams I've seen handle this well: standardize the CI environment so runs are genuinely comparable, get serious about dependency management instead of letting versions drift, and flag flaky tests early instead of letting them quietly pile up as "just re-run it."

What's the flakiest test you've ever fought with, and did you ever actually find the root cause?

#SoftwareTesting #CI #DevOps #SoftwareEngineering #TestAutomation #Backend

I don't use CLAUDE anymore in my test automation.

That's what I'd would have written couple a months ago.
AI broke all my tests and this was the point where I needed to handle CLAUDE better.

Here is what happended: Claude helped me get a suite green.
It was green. Fast. Perhaps too fast.

Than I looked closer on the Diff, on the changes.
What has happened? CLAUDE removed the assertions that stood in the way of making the suite green.
It has soften the tests, not fixed them.

It as well added hard waits, where it did not understand the business context, what was happening.
So no more flaky tests, green all the way.

But the critical code section in the test was soften so much, that it more or less did nothing the test.

This was my aha moment.
Quitting on AI was not an option. Every client wants it, needs it.
But understanding it better, the tools, the setup, how it works, this actually was the way.

Sometimes AI without boundaries and guards is too powerful.

The reason for this behavior is of course the limited context window, hallucinations and the drive to always reach the goal. No matter what. Green over truth.

Here are the rules I use now:
Always use a CLAUDE.md that defines what a test looks like and what not. That describes the coding standards and even explains the business logic where needed.
As well the usage of before and after hooks that enforce a controlled state. A guard script for these hooks which validates the assertions, so that a weakened check gets caught. (more on this on the next post).
And of course, always review the changes. Always!

What happened? What where the results?

CLAUDE is back in my test automations.
Faster and better than before.
No more weakening tests.

So no, I didn't stop using AI
But I stopped using CLAUDE without guardrails.

That was a big lesson for me to learn.

👉 Have you ever got such AI surprises? How did you handle it?

5,000 tests. A 0.1% flake rate per test.

That sounds excellent. It isn't.
Run the numbers.
0.1% per test across 5,000 tests produces 5 spurious failures per full run.
If the pipeline fails on any red test, the odds a clean build passes end to end are 0.999^5000.
That's 0.7%.
Your team will never see a green build caused by correctness. Only green builds caused by luck and retries.
And then the real damage starts.
Once engineers learn that red doesn't mean broken, the suite stops being a signal and becomes a tax.
Real defects hide in the noise. Escape rate climbs. Leadership concludes automation doesn't work. The investment gets cut. The escape rate climbs further.
This is the actual problem AI in testing should be solving.
Not "write my tests for me." That's the least valuable thing it does.
The expensive part was never authoring. It was years of maintenance, daily triage, and the slow erosion of trust.
In most orgs, time-to-triage dominates MTTR by a factor of five. That's the component worth attacking first, which is why failure classification and flake scoring pay off long before test generation does.
But here's the trap.
You're inserting a probabilistic component into a system whose entire job is producing a trustworthy binary signal.
Get that wrong and you haven't improved the suite. You've added a more confusing source of noise, harder to debug because its reasoning lives outside the source code.
One sentence governs the whole architecture:
Probabilistic components propose. Deterministic components verify. Humans approve anything irreversible.
If you can draw an arrow from your model straight to a merged commit, the architecture is broken.

posts.description:
The dangerous part of a flaky test isn't the false failure. It's what happens when teams stop investigating.

Google found that 𝟴𝟰% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀-𝘁𝗼-𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 they observed involved a flaky test.

At Google's scale, 𝟭𝟲% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.

So "probably just flaky" becomes a reasonable assumption - right up until it's wrong.

Nobody ignores a defect on purpose. But when false alarms happen often enough, teams learn to dismiss them.
And eventually, the excuse for a false alarm becomes indistinguishable from the excuse for a real regression.

That's where the risk sits.

If your release process can't distinguish the two, your test suite starts measuring confidence instead of quality.

The next time a test is labelled "𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗸𝘆," ask one question:
Did we prove it was flaky, or did it simply pass the second time?

posts.description:
"Works on my machine" is an answer. "Works in local, fails in CI" is a symptom.

The moment a developer sees a red pipeline and says "Ah, it's just a flaky QA test, just re-run it," the test suite has officially lost its value.

Quality isn't a gate at the end of the sprint that QA guards with a whip. If developers don't trust the automated suite, they won't look at the failures. And if they don't look at the failures, your CI pipeline is just an expensive electricity consumer.

Three rules to restore trust in your test suite:
Delete boat-anchor tests: If a test has been failing for two weeks and nobody cares, delete it. Git remembers.
Shift setup to API: Stop wasting 15 seconds per test clicking through login screens.
Zero tolerance for flakiness: Quarantine flaky tests immediately until they are fixed.

A suite of 20 reliable tests beats 200 flaky tests every single day.
How do you handle flaky builds in your team? Quarantine or infinite re-runs?

#DevOps #QA #Playwright #SoftwareQuality #Agile

posts.description:
There's a pattern that shows up once a test suite gets big enough. Every test wired straight to a live dependency. The real API, the shared staging box, the third-party sandbox. It feels honest. You're testing the real thing, right?

Then the provider has a rough morning and 200 tests go red. Not one of them caught a bug. They caught latency.

The fix we keep relearning is a seam. One layer you control, sitting between your tests and the outside world. A fake, an adapter, a contract test that pins down the provider's shape. Your tests talk to the seam. The seam talks to reality, on your terms.

It happens because direct wiring is the fastest thing to write. Realism now, flakiness later. And flaky tests cost more than time. They train people to ignore red, and that's the one thing a suite can't afford.

You still need real integration checks. Just not scattered across every unit test, one per provider.

Where's the line for you between a test that's realistic and one that's just coupled to someone else's uptime?

#CICD #DevOps #TestAutomation #FlakyTests

comments.author: li-user-61
comments.text:
Contract tests are the underrated middle ground here. They pin the provider's shape so you catch breaking changes without needing the provider live or inheriting its downtime. How do you keep those contracts from quietly going stale?

More on this here: https://dev.to/james_lin/tried-corsairdevcorsair-today-a-practical-gateway-test-drive-bd0

comments.author: li-user-63
comments.text: This is the exact failure mode CI/CD suites hit once they scale — one flaky third-party dependency and dozens of tests go red for reasons that have nothing to do with the code under test. Contract tests are underrated for this in API-heavy stacks (RestAssured is where they earn their keep most) since they pin the provider's shape without needing it live. The staleness question is the real open problem though — most teams only notice a contract drifted when the mock and the real integration test disagree.

posts.description:
I spent part of this week testing out Shiplight AI. It's a different take on AI test automation, and worth a look.

I used Claude + the Shiplight skill to create a few tests. What Shiplight gives you is a simple YAML test definition that captures the intent of the test, then transpiles that into Playwright underneath.

The interesting part is what happens when the app changes.

Instead of constantly fixing selectors and maintaining generated test code, Shiplight can re-resolve the right elements, regenerate the Playwright, and auto-fix a lot of the breakage, and the run keeps going, with nothing to commit.

So the tradeoff starts to change: more coverage doesn't have to mean more maintenance.

The YAML is also much easier to understand and review than the generated code, and you don't really have to write it by hand - your AI coding tool does that through the Shiplight skill.

It ships with a reporter too, so you can see failures, flaky tests, and why things broke.

Readable intent on top, Playwright underneath, with a lot less maintenance in between.

Cool product, do check it out!

You can try it for free today: https://lnkd.in/gyJarj37
